utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. And good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It won't be long. Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I hope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, one small matter. We have been informed by the Victim and Witnesses Unit that this witness would like to leave by 3.00 because he has a plane to catch, so I was hoping that Mr. Morrissey finishes cross-examination just -- and gives me just a few moments for my re-examination. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Morrissey, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And could I indicate to the witness, he will be comfortably finished. I have to point out to all in court, I'm acting for Mr. Halilovic here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Morrissey: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But yes -- pardon me, Mr. Okovic. We will finish quickly. Could I just ask you this -- you're quite a good car -- or at that time, were you quite a talented car driver at the time when the war was going on?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did you have to have experience in driving four-wheel-drive vehicles and all-terrain vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I've just got some questions for you about -- and the questions that remain, so that you know what's coming, I've got a couple of questions about your second day, that's the reconnaissance day that you talked about, when you went out with Zuka. And then I've got some questions about the third day, and I'm going to get you to put some marks on a photograph. And then I've got a couple of final questions concerning what happened after the third day, and then I'm finished. So that's what's coming. Now, turning to your second day, in other words, the day after you arrived, the day you went on reconnaissance, you indicated that you were in the company of Zulfikar Alispago on that day. You also indicated yesterday that when you came back from that long reconnaissance, that Zuka came became before you, either some minutes or some short period of time before you did. And what I wanted to ask you was: At that time, did you spend most of that day in the personal company of Zuka because he was the person to show you the terrain that you were going to look at?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I practically spent the time there from the morning until 9.00 at night, and I think that we were together practically all of that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. All right. Thank you. Well, that puts an end to that day. Now, I want to move to the following day, that is, the day after you arrived back and met Adnan Solakovic and heard all the terrible things or heard some of the terrible things that happened in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, could the witness please be shown a -- an exhibit, it's a photograph and it's Exhibit P4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a photograph that's going to be brought up on the screen there. And it's another view of the village of Grabovica that you have seen -- you've seen a different photograph. Now you're going to see one that's a little bit closer up. And while that's being brought up, I'll explain what I'd like you to do, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the photograph that's appeared on the screen, I believe, is P3. And it's P4 that I want, which is a slightly more close-up. Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have in front of you a photograph with -- in the top right-hand corner the numbers 0149-4609?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, this is a slightly more close-up picture than the one that you looked at before. Could I ask you, please -- the things I'm going to ask for here that you -- that you mark on this are, first of all, the -- the house where your command was set up, and then I'm going to ask you to indicate a couple of other houses. So do that one first, please.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's the house that's here, in this area. That's where this old railway station was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We're -- we're just having a little trouble getting that --

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've drawn a "1" on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I notice I've been going very fast, so I'll slow down a little bit here. Now, could you indicate by drawing a line whereabouts was the original checkpoint where your soldiers were. In other words, you remember when you came back from your reconnaissance in the middle of the night and you saw a soldier there on guard? Was there -- was that soldier at a checkpoint, or was he just simply on guard at the house?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My soldier was in front of the house. The guard from my unit was in front of the house, not at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Very well. Okay. Now, the next thing I want you to mark on the map is the point where the -- the second house where your 2nd Independent Battalion soldiers were before you pulled them back to safety.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want you --

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Okay. And just to be clear, you see your red circle there has captured one and a half houses, so I just want to ask you, do you see you've -- you've got a part to have roof of -- of a house down near the --

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You've now put a cross on that -- on a house, and that cross indicates -- that's not the house you're talking about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, no. The house is on the hill. That's the house where my soldiers were billeted. This house was damaged. This photograph is only two or three years old, so that the whole terrain has changed. The wood processing plant wasn't there and all the greenery now is much more -- it's much bigger. So you can't really see the house. But I know that the house was there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of what you've said about the scenery changing, I'm going to show you another photograph in a minute. But I still need this photograph now to get you to mark something more. Could you please mark on this map now where it was that the new checkpoint appeared. Now, you remember saying yesterday that after you pulled your soldiers back, I asked you whether you saw another checkpoint spring up, and you indicated "yes." Would you please indicate where on that map this new checkpoint appeared.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've marked it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- okay. The letters -- you've marked it with a "C" and "P" to indicate "checkpoint"?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Checkpoint, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Excellent. And those checkpoints went up after you had withdrawn your men back to the safety of house marked number "1"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I offer that document for tender, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there's no objections from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Defence Exhibit D274.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to the court staff. D274.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you one more photograph now, and that is Exhibit P7. This will be a closer-up version of part of that photograph. Okay. Do you have in front of you with photograph with the numbers 0149-4612 in the top corner?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excellent. Would you please mark on that photograph the house in which your soldiers were billeted before you pulled them back to the -- to the safety of the command house.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the house. It's marked with a number "2".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we're just having a little bit of technical trouble here, which we'll resolve swiftly. Thank you. We now have it. Very well. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just have a question for you about that house: Do you recall whether or not there were any women living in that house at any time when you were in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that house was empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Would you please draw on this -- on that picture where the checkpoint was that was put up at a later stage and mark it with "CP."

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] I think that he was there, the -- I don't know whether it was in front of the house or behind the house, but that's where the damaged structure was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I offer that document for tender as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Defence Exhibit D275.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I just have a handful of questions remaining now. We're still on the day after you returned from your reconnaissance, and -- and in relation to that day, I just wanted to ask you a question: Do you recall a man named Namik Dzankovic arriving at your command post or your -- when I say "command post," at your -- at your command house, at the railway station, at any stage during that particular day?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing him. I don't know whether it was that day or not. And we probably just greeted each other, said hello, because we've known each other. I know that man. I don't know whether that was on that particular day. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I just want to ask you just one question about -- about him: Whether you heard Namik Dzankovic ask any questions concerning the deaths of civilians when you saw him.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him, was Adnan Solakovic present or not, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we were together, the whole of the command of my unit was together when he came, and we just said hello.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. All right. When you say that you know Namik Dzankovic, I take it you know him as a pretty straightforward honest sort of person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't consider everyone to be a friend, but he is among those that I do consider to be my friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And just following from that, so far as you know him, you've always known him to be a pretty honest and straightforward person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The final questions are -- that I have concern this individual that you've referred to, Caco, Musan Topalovic. You saw him behaving in an apparently callous way towards a -- a dead body after the meeting at Jablanica. But it wasn't until that time that you saw units -- either Caco or -- well, perhaps I'll withdraw that question. You were unable to put a date on -- on when you saw Caco, but it was after -- it was on the way back from the meeting at Jablanica, wasn't it, when you saw Caco dealing with this particular body?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And after that time, you saw certain -- certain people associated with Caco's unit in the area of the Neretva, including in Grabovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not before that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not before that time. I saw him in that area at that time, but naturally before that I used to see him in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I understand that. But the first time -- sorry, it wasn't until after that body-burning episode or attempted body-burning episode that you saw Caco in units of the 10th Brigade in the vicinity of the Grabovica; that's accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. That completes the cross-examination. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect, Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Your Honours. Thank you, Your Honours. Re-examined by Ms. Chana:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one or two questions. I wanted to ask you about that day. That would be the -- the second day, and that was the day you went on the reconnaissance mission. Now, can you remember what time was it that Zuka left wherever you were and -- to go back to Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we left the place where we were doing the reconnaissance together, and then I think one of my company commanders called Ibro hurt his foot slightly, so we lagged behind somewhat, so that he probably arrived about half an hour at Donja Jablanica before I did. And this is actually the only reason why we came back half an hour later from reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And remind us again what time you -- you did come back from reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was late at night. It was night. It was between 9.00 and 10.00 when we arrived at Donja Jablanica. That was about the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during your cross-examination, counsel for the Defence asked you about how the soldiers were behaving towards the civilians. Now, did you go around the village to notice how they were behaving? What was your movement patterns when you were -- when you arrived in the village of Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which soldiers are you thinking of? The soldiers under my command or soldiers of some other unit?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you were -- generally you said that the soldiers -- when you arrived in Grabovica, the soldiers were behaving very well to the civilians, and you had agreed with that, and that's the clarification that I seek.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go around to observe?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yes, I didn't understand the question. My soldiers behaved properly towards the civilians that we found in the village. There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, other soldiers, when they came, then what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That will be all from this witness, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Judge El Mahdi, please. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, this is just checking on a little point. You said that on the 8th of September you received -- you were visited by several officers, in particular Mr. Karic. And my question is the following: Where was this conversation? Where did it happen?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held at our provisional command at the old railway station. Vehbija Karic was present with two other high-ranking officers from the Main Staff. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. And the other troops, were they all from your own battalion, or did you have all the other troops who were there in Grabovica, were around?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, only our unit was present in Grabovica. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Right. So on that same day you went to Konjic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Therefore, for the conversation which took place on that evening, you said that Mr. Halilovic had been present and that it was he who had given all the tasks -- indicated all the tasks for each battalion.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said it like that. As the most senior-ranking officer in that room, Mr. Halilovic - well, I could put it in a nonmilitary way - who was chairing that meeting, just explained the significance of the operation for the liberation of the road towards Mostar, while lower-ranking officers actually did what you are asking me about in the question. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. And did he give a code name to this operation?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR OKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the Defence of People's Rights 93. That was the name of the operation, as far as I can remember. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's question? It seems to me none. At this stage, are there any documents that need to be tendered? No, I don't think so. Well, Witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. Madam Usher will show you out of the room and we wish you a very pleasant journey back home. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that we still have some time, so maybe it's the proper time for us to discuss the filings or submissions from the Prosecution concerning of the 89(F) witnesses. Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, despite my bold claim yesterday that I would be ready today, the Prosecutors, I think, worked very hard and got something to us by e-mail at lunchtime today. I'm not sure if the Court is aware of what the situation is is in the Defence room, but there's six computer terminals and six teams with about 30 people competing for use there. The news is not all bad, as far as delay goes, I can indicate. I can't respond yet to everything that's been raised or to the matter generally. But Mr. Kapur is the witness who needs to be resolved swiftly, and I may hand over to my learned friend Mr. Mettraux, who's taking that witness in cross-examination. We've had a think about our position about that and we may be able to accommodate to some degree what the Prosecution says. May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- sorry, perhaps before I do that -- so, I apologise to the Court, I don't have a general answer yet because I think the Prosecution have behaved in good faith and tried hard to get it to us. We only had an hour and as it happened we wouldn't -- I still haven't seen it. But they did send it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we could just deal with one witness first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honour. The Defence will not object to the admission of the evidence in chief of that witness through Rule 89(F). There's a number of things, however, that we would like to clarify at this stage. And the first matter concerns the clarification given yesterday by Mr. Re in relation to one particular paragraph contained in the Rule 89(F) of the witness, and the Defence takes the view that that specific paragraph does not go to the acts and conduct of the accused insofar as the charges are concerned and that, as a matter of fact, it is irrelevant to the present charges. So that is essentially the basis for our not Octobers to the evidence in chief going through 89(F). The second matter which the Defence would like to point out at this stage are matter which is we've already pointed out in relation to Mr. Saban Neziric, the previous witness, which was put forth as a Rule 89(F) witness. We've indicated at the time that we considered the right of Mr. Halilovic to a public trial to be a very important right and that there was a public interest as well to having a public trial, and we stand and reiterate that submission. We also reiterate our position that the scope of permissible re-examination in a situation where the evidence in chief has been put forward as Rule 89(F) should be interpreted particularly strictly. And finally, also a matter that we've raised with Mr. Neziric is the lesser weight to be given to evidence submitted in that form. And finally, there is one matter of some concern to the Defence, which is the practice by the Prosecution of taking new witness statements for the purpose of 89(F), and it is the Defence understanding that once the Prosecution has decided to put forward or to put forth the evidence in chief in the form of a written statement, it should be done in the form of the existing statement. If the Prosecution for one reason or another has some doubt as to the reliability of those statements, it should not be permitted to proceed under Rule 89(F). There is a risk, which was highlighted, I think, by Judge Hunt in his dissenting opinion in the Milosevic case that "a party putting such a statement forward would perhaps unintentionally but put the best gloss possible on the evidence, which would in essence distort the reality or the nature of that witness evidence and it is a risk that we are particularly sensitive to, and we think that from the moment when the Prosecution has decided that a witness should be put forth as 89(F) witness, there should be no need, nor any necessity for the Prosecution to have further proofing. And that will be all of our submissions as far as this matter is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any response, Mr. Ray.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, there-most certainly is. On two particular points. The first point is the right to a public trial. I have no idea why the Defence is raising that. It is of course a public trial. 89(F) provides that evidence may be given orally or in written form according to the interests of justice. The interests of justice may allow a witness to give evidence in written form. The witness is here for cross-examination. It is the -- the evidence is public, it's a tendered statement. It is released to the public. They are cross-examined on it, and I will read a short summary of the contents of that -- of the 89(F) statement. So that covers the first point. The second point, in my respectful submission, is the point my learned friend raises about us not putting a new document -- a new document in the sense of a comprehensive document containing the witness's evidence to the Trial Chamber. It's quite frankly nonsensical. The situation is often witnesses may have been interviewed over a lengthy period, given interviews to investigators or lawyers from various entities, international and domestic. That evidence would be given orally before the Trial Chamber. Is my learned friend seriously suggesting in -- in relation to a witness we would put four or five statements, maybe taken over five years or ten years, together, and just hand them up to the Trial Chamber and say to them, "Please, Your Honours, we -- we appreciate that a lot of this is going to be irrelevant, but we're just going to ask you to try and work out for yourself what is relevant and what is irrelevant"? It is particularly germane in this particular trial where the Defence daily raises complaint about the behaviour or misconduct, as they characterise it, of the former lead investigator in this case, Mr. Mikhailov, Nikolai Mikhailov. The statement of Mr. Kapur and many other witnesses was in fact taken by Mr. Mikhailov. This particular statement was not a bad one. However, there were two particular statements in relation to Mr. Kapur: One given to Bosnian authorities, some of which he says was not correct, and some -- and one given to us. The most logical, most practical, and the most efficacious way of presenting the evidence is to prepare a document which encapsulates the entirety of the witness's evidence and to do it in a professional manner and to have the lawyer who is in fact leading the evidence do it. In this sense, it is no different to in domestic proceedings where -- or any domestic proceedings where evidence is taken by statement. In civil proceedings and domestic countries it is normal and it is done in an affidavit, which is tendered before the Court and cross-examination is allowed. The situation is no different here, and the Prosecution submits that the -- the most reliable way of getting the evidence before the Court is to prepare a proper document setting it all out, have the witness sign it, if possible in two languages, and then tender that. Otherwise, real problems of practicality, reliability, and relevance arise as to what we're putting before the Trial Chamber, and we want to ensure we have the most relevant, the most probative, and the briefest -- the briefest document we could possibly -- the briefest thing we could possibly put before the Trial Chamber. So we strongly resist the last suggestion my learned friend made us tendering multiple documents taken over many years before the Trial Chamber. And in relation to re-examination, I would say -- my submission is it is no different from the evidence of any other witness, whether it's oral or written. And finally, my learned friend has made a submission that the evidence of a witness given in chief, pursuant to 89(F), should somehow be treated in a different manner by the Trial Chamber to that of a witness giving their evidence live. If the Defence is going to make that submission the Prosecution would invite the Trial Chamber to inform us now whether that is in fact the Trial Chamber's view that less weight is to be given to the evidence of a witness who gives their evidence in writing or -- and adopts it, and whether in a judgement Your Honours will -- will find that the evidence should be treated differently. Because if that's the case, the Prosecution will withdraw its application to call any evidence under 89(F) and we'll submit that all evidence should be given orally, if that is the Trial Chamber's view. So we invite the Trial Chamber to -- to give us an advance ruling on your attitude towards the Defence submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any comments or response?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: In relation to this particular witness -- I mean, we have indicated that we would be ready to proceed upon 89(F) and we indeed are. The only matter which I would like very briefly to reply to is indeed the confirmation that the basis upon which the summary which is provided to the Chamber seems to be open to some question. My learned colleague has indicated the allegations made by the Defence in relation to the misconduct of their investigator. The other matter which relates to that -- directly to that witness is his own admission in his OTP statement to have been threatened and otherwise abused during the taking of his 1993 statement. And part of the evidence received at the time now forms part of the document which is put before the Trial Chamber. We -- we strongly believe that in situations where there are doubts as to the reliability of the statements in question, the evidence of the witness in chief should be taken live. As for the suggestion that several -- or many statements should be put before the Trial Chamber, this is not our position. We believe that if the Prosecution intends to proceed pursuant to Rule 89(F), they have the opportunity to put solely the OTP statements of which generally there are one, two, or tree such statements and to proceed in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that there are two issues which need the Bench to address at this stage. The first one is about the so-called many statements. It is a practice according to the Rule 89(F) that a statement will be admitted into the evidence after the testimony of this witness. But as the Prosecution pointed out that the person may make a lot of statements concerning the same matter in the past few years and there are a lot of irrelevant issues mentioned in that statement. We hope that the Prosecution could somehow redact the statement and discuss it with the Defence. The Trial Chamber will admit that redacted statement into the evidence. The second issue is about the different weight. Here the Bench could not agree with the propositions made by the Defence that the evidence introduced through 89(F) should be given less weight. We all understand that the evidence introduced through 92 bis without cross-examination needs some corroboration, which means that the evidence introduced according to 92 bis without cross-examination has less weight than the evidence introduced through the 92 bis with the cross-examination. Here we believe that the right of the accused for a fair and expeditious trial is fully guaranteed by applying the 89(F) with the cross-examination, so we could not agree with the Defence that this kind of evidence should be given less weight in the elaboration of those evidence in the future. We notice that the Defence does not object to the application of the Prosecution to hear the witness and to have his testimony admitted into the Rule 89(F) concerning with the next witness. The Trial Chamber in full recognition to the rights of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial and considers it in the interests of justice to grant the Prosecution's application to have the next witness testimony admitted through Rule 89(F). It is so decided. Could we have the next witness, please. And by the way, Mr. Morrissey, are we in the position to discuss with the rest of the witnesses tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the answer to that is yes because the Prosecutor has -- has filed something, and the fact that I failed to look at it can be rectified pretty quickly, so I think we can, Your Honour. And I think -- depending on how fast Mr. Kapur goes, can I indicate we'll probably get to the next witness, Mr. Zebic, in respect of whom there may be some legal discussions before we start. But it may be that we'll be part heard with Mr. Zebic and then when he finishes, that might be an opportune moment to -- as I expect him to finish at some stage tomorrow, maybe after an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that we'll find some time between the witnesses to discuss all those matters, like we did right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, could we have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kapur. Is your name -- full name Kemo Kapur?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your date of birth is the 25th of February, 1967? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant 1965. I'm sorry. And your occupation --

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- is a judge of the municipal court in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1993, you were the chief of the military police company in the 9th Motorised Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you two documents, one in English and one in B/C/S. Just have a look at those two documents. Look at the one in B/C/S. Is it a statement you signed yesterday of eight pages relating to the matters in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the statement in English, is that the English version, and you've also signed that?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are the contents of that statement true and correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May those documents be received into evidence as the evidence of this witness pursuant to Rule 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P276.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For the purposes of the -- for the Trial Chamber's benefit and to -- for the purposes of the public proceedings, I'll just read a brief summary of the contents of the witness's evidence onto the record. In 1993, the witness was the chief of the military police company of the 9th Motorised Brigade and was so until Operation Trebevic on the 26th of October, 1993. In the summer of 1993, he became aware that soldiers from the assault company of the 9th Motorised Brigade were introducing themselves as military police and extorting money from civilians in Sarajevo. They were taking civilians, mainly business people, such as cafe owners, into custody and demanding "donations" from them for the 9th Motorised Brigade. His Rule 98(F) [sic] statement provides specific examples of this. One member of the brigade, Mustafa Hota, stole an UNPROFOR vehicle. The witness is unaware whether Hota was investigated or punished for it. Soldiers of the 9th were also going - assault company - were also going to the Markale marketplace in Sarajevo, introducing themselves as military police, and taking civilians to the front line to dig -- lines to dig trenches. Judge Kapur himself twice saw Mustafa Hota, Ertan Hukelic, and Foca Kenan, and some other soldiers making civilians get onto a truck and taking them to the front line. The witness is aware that the 10th Mountain Brigade was doing the same but in a worse manner. At the front lines, military police stood between the civilians and the enemy while they were digging the trenches. In early July 1993, soldiers from the assault company blocked -- that's the 9th Motorised Brigade's assault company, blockaded the ABiH Supreme Command in Central Sarajevo and blocked and attacked a police station, also disarming central -- the civilian police in Central Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slowly -- read more slowly for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will. The military police did not participate in this but Ramiz Delalic ordered Mr. Kapur to secure the military police headquarters on the first night. Mr. Kapur himself ordered the release of two civilian police, who had been taken into custody by members of the assault company. The blockade ended after Ramiz Delalic and Musan Topalovic, that's Caco, reached an agreement with President Izetbegovic about personal changes in the military. Mr. Kapur was aware that members of the 9th Assault Company and the 2nd Independent Battalion, including Adnan Solakovic, and the 10th Mountain Brigade's assault unit, including Topalovic, was sent to Herzegovina in September 1993 in an operation he later heard was called "Neretva." No military police from the 9th accompanied them. He was not asked to investigate any allegations in relation to Grabovica and the murders upon their return. Ramiz Delalic, that is, Celo, the 9th Motorised Brigade deputy commander spent all of his time -- spent most of his time at the headquarters of the assault company commanded by Malco Rovcanin. He had his office there and slept there. Daily meetings of the 9th Motorised Brigade subordinate commanders occurred every morning in the brigade headquarters. Sefer Halilovic attended one such meeting when he was the Chief of Staff in 1993 for about half an hour. Mr. Kapur does not remember what was discussed on that day. That's the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination? Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Mettraux:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kapur. My name is Guenael Mettraux and I appear as co-counsel on behalf of Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 9th Motorised Brigade of which you were a member, sir, was a strong unit in the ABiH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was also a brigade that was most important to the defence of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And many of the soldiers who later become members of the 9th Brigade were among the first in Sarajevo to have taken up arms to defend the city; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And first among those was the man who would become the deputy commander, Ramiz Delalic, Celo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reputation which the 9th Motorised Brigade had acquired as a good fighting unit explained the fact that it was later sent to fight outside of Sarajevo, including on Mount Igman, where there was a particular need for strong and mobile units; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And although Celo or Ramiz Delalic was rumoured to have a rather colourful past, the brigade as a whole had a good reputation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was no criminal brigade, as some have tried to portray it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean it is correct it was not a criminal brigade; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: The brigade was certainly not; although, individuals probably were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We will come to that matter a little bit later. You yourself, sir, would not have accepted to be part of a criminal group. You would have refused to become a member of such a group.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, it was a very patriotic unit, one you were proud to be a member of.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Absolutely. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've just pointed out, sir, it was not a perfect unit. It also had its problems. It had its good and its bad soldiers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: There were very few bad soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And among those rather, I would say, colourful characters were two individuals called Musa Hota -- Mustafa Hota and Kenan Foco; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And although those two did not shine in their respect, I should say, for their -- for their military regulation and military discipline, they nevertheless showed great courage in combat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I never participated in any fighting together with them, so I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But would you know, for instance, that Mr. Hota, Musa Hota, got injured when he bravely was the first to walk through the enemy front line and walked -- or stepped on a line and got very serious injuries as a result? Are you aware of that incident, sir?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I -- no, I haven't heard about that incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's okay. And you would agree, sir, that Mr. Hota, knowing who he is, would not have been the first choice in a military cadet school?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I -- objection to that. I don't quite understand what the question is, what it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Is that related to our case?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It will become with the next question. I'm -- but I will -- I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, sir, Sarajevo was encircled by Serbian forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Serbian forces up the hills around Sarajevo didn't show much respect for the laws of war; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: It's well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution understands what the Defence says and where they're going. The attitude towards the Serbian forces towards the laws of war are entirely relevant to allegations about what happened in Grabovica and Uzdol and the reputation of the 9th and the 10th for criminality or otherwise. There's no tu quoque if it's coming close to that here. And we object to this line of cross-examination as to what the Serbian soldiers were doing. What's the relevance to -- to the allegations against Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, well, here I don't think the Defence counsel is talking about the attitude of the Serb soldiers; just to lay the background for the situation which will lead to something happened in Sarajevo under the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I may reassure my colleague. We are not running a tu quoque defence in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your understanding, sir, it was the clear intention of the Serbian forces to take the town of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's common knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time the Bosnian army would need any able-bodied men who were brave or otherwise willing to fight on behalf of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've already said, sir, that although the 9th Motorised Brigade might not be a model brigade, it was no worse or for that matter no worse than other brigades in Sarajevo at the time; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the truth is, sir, that prior to September 1993 you were not aware of any serious criminal offences having been committed by any members of the 9th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, would you agree -- or I will put it otherwise. Would it be correct to describe the 9th Brigade as generally a morally sound entity and one that was praised many times, including by the president of the state, Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that a fact, sir, that some of the rumours which circulated in Sarajevo as to the reputation of the 9th Brigade were the result of jealousies or tensions between certain brigades and certain units, for instance, of the MUP, or Ministry of the Interior? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that they were in fact or in part the result of Caco and Celo having been particularly vocal and critical about some MUP units which did not take much part in the defence of the town, although they were well armed? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a number of those rumours had to do with the deputy commander, Celo himself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you can tell and as far as you can indicate to this Court, Celo was a strong fighter.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a brave one.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Very brave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that I'm clear, sir, about one small matter: The nickname of Ramiz Delalic was Celo. Could you tell this Trial Chamber what this means in your language, "Celo."

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: It means "without hair," a person who doesn't have any hair on their head. They're bald.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct to suggest that Ramiz Delalic, Celo, is suffering from this common affliction of balding? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he have receding hair, which would explain his nickname?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Is that correct, sir, to suggest that Celo did not have much of a military education at the time?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it also be correct to suggest that he was more interested in doing his duty, defending the town, than ponder the finesses of military regulations? Is that correct? He was a practical man?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps among all of those who can take some credit in defending the city, he may be among the bravest; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Celo was not a perfect commander, but would it be correct to suggest that he would not tolerate illegal activities or misdemeanours within his brigade? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: To a degree that is correct. He frequently criticised those people who committed minor misdemeanours or criminal acts, and he punished them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, you've indicated to the Prosecution in your statement that on a number of occasions he took certain measures when he learned about those minor offences or misdemeanours to punish them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also indicated that on a number of occasions Celo would take certain, what I could call, shortcuts in doing so. He would detain the person and the decision which should by law have been rendered prior to detention would be rendered afterwards. Is that the way he would operate?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct, sir, to suggest that Celo would not entrust it to anyone else -- please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. Just one short digression. This is not a military prison. This is just military detention as part -- with the military police company that I commanded over. And a specific example also: On one occasion, he found out that two members of the assault company seized money from a civilian, and he personally brought those people in. He detained them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm grateful for this clarification and I apologise if I misled you. Thank you for that. Would it also be fair to suggest that Celo would not entrust it to anyone else to deal with serious problems within the brigade? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Could you please clarify your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm trying to understand or perhaps I will put it that way to you: Celo was extremely protective of his own men, of the members of the 9th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he considered that no one outside of the brigade should interfere with those men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: It's relatively correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's correct to suggest that within the -- or that he treated or regarded the 9th Brigade as his personal fiefdom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you describe the way he was treating the 9th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: He was the deputy commander of the brigade, first of all. It's true that he protected fighters who directly participated in armed combat by that brigade. When they were going straight to the front, not once when I was present would he allow any soldier to go beyond the line of risk until he personally had carried out reconnaissance. Within the brigade, he always suggested that the soldiers who had -- who directly participated in combat be rewarded. On the other hand, he didn't like those people who worked in the offices doing administrative work. And in that way, he protected and in a way promoted those members who took part in actions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm grateful for this explanation. Would it be correct that -- to say, to take on your last point, to say that he liked the sort soldiers that he was, brave, practical men? He didn't like JNA officers -- office -- soldiers, I think as you called them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this practical approach of his and the courage he showed in combat endeared him with the local population and with his soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, the inhabitants of Stari Grad, which is the part of Sarajevo or parts of Sarajevo which he defended, petitioned the army so that Celo would be appointed as commander of the brigade. As you've indicated, it was not -- it did not happen. But that's what happened, isn't it? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, perhaps because of this too great popularity and perhaps also because of his lack of military experience, his appointment as a brigade commander was refused; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you know, however, is that Mr. Sulejman or Suljo Imsirovic was appointed as commander of the brigade and not Mr. Delalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that Mr. Imsirovic was one of those former JNA officers whom Mr. Delalic didn't like too much; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps as a result of this dislike, there came a time when Celo decided to ban Mr. Imsirovic from entering his own headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me. This happened only once, on one occasion. This was not something that happened on a regular basis, but in one instance there was some kind of misunderstanding when he said that the brigade commander should not be allowed to enter the premises of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And it was rather difficult, wasn't it, to try to resist Celo when he decided to do something or not to do something; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you attempted on a number of occasions to stand up to him, but it was most of the time -- or to make proposals to him, but it was rather difficult, as in the instance of the arrest of Kijabe Zahib [phoen], which you've explained in your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I -- I'm not familiar with that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- the name is Nedzad Burovic, can you remember that incident, sir?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember the attitude of Mr. Delalic, Celo, on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I can explain. I remember that specific case. What happened was that Musa Hota literally seized a vehicle from this gentleman, Nedzad Burovic. He simply took the vehicle. Mr. Burovic contacted me, as the commander of the military police, because a cousin of his was a member of the military police unit. I informed Delalic about this and requested that the vehicle be returned to the gentleman. Delalic agreed to this, that the vehicle be returned; however, because Burovic was a civilian, he said that he should go and dig trenches for a day and then the vehicle would be returned to him, and this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that occasion, sir, he also warned you -- or told you not to intervene ever again in those matters, even if you were asked to do so by Alija Izetbegovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it also be correct, sir, to suggest that Celo, Ramiz Delalic, was someone one had to convince or negotiate with? That was the way to handle him, try to convince him.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's what you experienced yourself when you were dealing with him.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like now, sir, to discuss another aspect of your evidence given in the form of a statement to the Prosecution, which concerned the so-called donations to the 9th Brigade. Would it be correct to suggest that at the time in 1992 and in 1993 there was very little money available in the army, in the ABiH army? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was also a desperate need at the time to buy weapons and ammunition; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was crucial to the defence of Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That was a generally known thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was also a desperate need at the time, sir, to obtain medical supplies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was also a need at the time to pay for the pensions of the soldiers who had been injured in combat and to their family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: These were not pensions, because there was no money then. But it was more assistance in food and medicines. We made packages in our units, and then we would take them to the wounded fighters or to their families so that they could get by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, sir. And it is correct that a number of members of the 9th Brigade took it upon themselves to collect money to pay for those things; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. This wasn't done by the majority of the brigade members. It was actually something that only the minority of the brigade members did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful for that. We must have been lost in translation. I didn't intend to suggest that a large number of them but only a very limited number of individuals were involved in -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that money, sir, was collected from people who -- those people who collected the money considered to be war profiteers, people who would not take part in the defence of the city but would do business during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is also a fact, sir, that because they were uncertain as to whether Celo or, for that matter, any other military commander might agree with what they were doing, they took a number of measures to hide their activities and to give it an appearance of legality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it's not -- it's not very clear. I will start with -- perhaps put the next question to you. Isn't it a fact, sir, that when certain members of the 9th Brigade collected money from businessmen and so on, they would generally give them -- or they would give them certificates for their so-called donation? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they would also generally claim to be members of the military police; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as a result of the money which was collected by some of those individuals, the 9th Brigade became one of the strongest and one of the best-armed units in the ABiH; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I really don't know that. The term "B and H army" is a broad term. I know the situation in Sarajevo. I didn't leave Sarajevo, so I know a little bit about Igman, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you to correct me. Would that be correct in relation to the troops which were based in Sarajevo, sir?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: We were solidly equipped, as far as weapons are concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that a fact also, sir, that when this cavalier methods of some of the members of the 9th Brigade came to light, it was regarded as unacceptable and it was decided that it should be regulated? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, a proposal was put forward to create a commission to deal with legal donations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, sir, as well as Dzevad Kasumovic, the chief of the brigade, an individual call Budva, who was in charge, I believe, of the kitchen, also became members of this three-persons commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: This wasn't put on paper formally, to have a commission for those purposes. But those two gentlemen suggested to me one day that we should go and see two owners of restaurants who of their own volition had expressed the desire to help the command. So people who had restaurants during the war and who proposed themselves that they would give a certain quantity of money would receive a receipt or a diploma as a form of gratitude for their donations to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And no coercion, sir, was used to have those people give any money to this three-persons commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir -- yes.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Just one moment. I would like to clarify something. They didn't give this money to us. They took the money to the brigade command, to the assistant commander for logistics in the command office. They would give the money there and would receive receipts for that in return. I'm sure that these donors were recorded in the archives, which must exist to this day. So there is a record of them and receipts of them as donors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm grateful for that, sir. Sir, are you aware, either from your personal knowledge or from the medias at the time, that Ramiz Delalic, Celo, was charged in 1994 allegedly for taking part in these so-called illegal donations and that he was in fact acquitted? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's take a break, and we'll resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to take you now to a different aspect of -- of the evidence which you gave to the Prosecution in your statement, and that relates to the digging of trenches around Sarajevo. Would I be correct -- or would it be correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just please -- I object to the form of the question. It's not a statement. The -- my learned friend keeps saying this. It's not a statement he gave to the Prosecution. It is his evidence before the Trial Chamber. I kindly ask my learned friend to refer to the exhibit which is the witness's evidence as his evidence to the Trial Chamber, not a statement he gave to the Prosecution. That's not what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm happy to refer to it as the evidence. But as the time when the witness signed the statement, it was a statement. It only became evidence when it was admitted by the Trial Chamber. So as far as it is concerned, it was a statement. But I will refer to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I -- let's not mention anything about that. Just take us to the incidents that happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would it be correct to suggest that the digging of trenches around Sarajevo was necessary at the time to protect the city?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain in -- in a few words perhaps the importance of such protective mechanism, the trenches, that is.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: As is well known, the enemy lines were very close to the city, so it was important to dig trenches in order to protect the soldiers who were manning these lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be correct to suggest that although a number of people in Sarajevo disapproved of the method which was used to dig those trenches, everyone saw the merit and the need for such trenches? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And interpreter's correction: The soldiers who were manning the lines protecting the city.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can clarify the situation. Later it turned out that it was essential to dig trenches and civilians were engaged via the civilian organs to trench-digging duty. Perhaps the way this was done wasn't the best possible way, the way it was done in 1993, the way it was done by the 9th and 10th Brigades. But later it turned out to be something essential because civilians through civilian organs who were not mobilised and who were on -- engaged on work duty were also engaged on trench-digging activities in order to protect the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you the for that. So would it be a fair summary to say that everyone was glad that such trenches were dug --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Objection to this. This is the second time my learned friend has said "everyone." Who is everyone? The citizens of Sarajevo? The witness and his family and his friends? He should be specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to suggest that the citizens or the people living in Sarajevo at the time were glad that such trenches had been dug but that no one really wanted to dig them? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct, sir, that Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks were taken to dig those trenches?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That is correct, all together. Meaning Bosniaks, Serbs, Croats, and Jews, and everybody who was not militarily engaged at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware, sir, of the fact that a number of -- a number of family members of Mr. Halilovic themselves were taken to dig trenches? Is that something you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've indicated in your evidence in chief before this Trial Chamber that it was not your duty as a military policeman to report any illegal activities or misdemeanours occurring in the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Only within the 9th Motorised Brigade, as part of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, thank you very much. Is it -- is it also correct to suggest that the main function of the military police of which you were a member were, first, to guard commanding posts and other important locations? Was it one of your main functions?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also to carry out patrols?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To carry out requisitioning activities?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Could you please clarify these requisitioning activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were there times when the military police were asked to obtain material -- logistical material for other units? Is that something you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And did members of the military police company ever take part in military operations? And I mean as combatants.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've pointed out earlier, sir, that it was not your duty to report -- by law to report any illegal activities of which you would have become aware, but is that correct that on a number of occasions you raised it nevertheless with your superior, Mr. Tomo Juric?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: If I can clarify the situation. As part of the military police company, there was -- we didn't possess any rules of conduct, nothing which would govern the conduct of members of the military police. Since I was a lawyer by profession before the war, I insisted that the detention as a -- within the brigade should be something that would be regulated, the way this detention should be applied. And as company commander, I allocated a military police officer who would be in charge of detention and the way it was run. Daily I made reports about the work and the activities of the military police, and I sent them on to the command -- brigade command, to Tomislav Juric, as deputy commander for security. A copy of the report was taken by messenger to the General Staff military security sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, sir, it would have been for Tomo Juric to forward those reports up the chain of command, if he -- if he had seen fit to do so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so that I'm clear about your duties as far as illegal activities or misdemeanours, as you've -- as you've qualified them, are concerned, your obligations were limited to that detention facility which you've discussed a minute ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mad no obligation to investigate crime and you had been given no resources or facilities to do so in any case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've indicated earlier that the 9th Brigade was an important piece of the defence of Sarajevo, and as such, a number of important people came to visit your headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that headquarters was located in Trampina Street in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And among the visitors that came to the headquarters of the 9th Brigade was, for instance, the president himself, Alija Izetbegovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that a number of ministers came to visit the brigade?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I'm not aware that they visited the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: High-ranking army officers came to visit the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going chronologically, I would like to discuss an incident which took place in the early days of July 1993. You've explained that the 9th Brigade surrounded a number of police stations in their zone of responsibility as well as the Supreme Command or the Main Staff of the army and that a number of police officers were disarmed as part of this blockade, so to say; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you could say, those police stations which were surrounded and the Main Staff, were not attacked, in the sense that there was no shoot-out, no exchange of fire between the police and the -- and the members of the 9th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I must clarify. I was not present on the spot, and I did not see how these policemen were disarmed and brought in. It is well known that there was only one police station in the old town, Stari Grad. I didn't see how that was blocked. I just heard from other soldiers that members of our brigade together with members of the 10th Motorised Brigade, Caco's brigade, that they disarmed some policemen and arrived at the eternal flame. The eternal flame is very far from the headquarters of the main command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as far as you heard -- I'm not suggesting that you saw it yourself. But as far as you were told, no one was hurt, no one was injured during the blockading and surrounding of the police station and the Main Staff. No one was hurt by members of the 9th Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apparently that whole incident was triggered by the mistrust which existed between the 9th Brigade and the MUP, on the one hand, and more specifically by a rumour spread by Musa Hota and Kenan Foco that the 9th Brigade was about to be attacked by the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've also indicated that the incident came to an end and that the siege of both the Main Staff and the police station was lifted after Caco and Celo had reached an agreement with Alija Izetbegovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I heard that from other soldiers.
