utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also heard that the condition put by Caco and Celo to the lifting of the siege was the replacement of a number of individuals from their position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I heard that too, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two individuals concerned, the two individuals which the -- which Caco and Celo requested to be removed were respectively Fikret Muslimovic and Mr. Hajrulahovic, known as Talijan; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I heard only about Fikret Muslimovic. I didn't hear about Talijan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what the position of Mr. Muslimovic was at the time, sir.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I think at the time he was the chief of security at the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a fact, isn't it, that shortly thereafter Mr. Muslimovic was removed and replaced by Mr. Jasarevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the -- you've indicated that the 9th Brigade is a rather large entity. There was about 5.000 men in whole in the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I think there were about 3.000 men approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was a multi-ethnic brigade. There were Serbs, Croats, Bosniaks in the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within that brigade, there were a number of battalions. And please correct me if I make my mistake in that respect. There were five battalions, composed each of three companies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in addition to those, there were a number of additional companies. There was, for instance, the military police company, of which you were a member.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... company.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and a --

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Engineering company.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And two or three artillery companies.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I think there was one artillery company. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, considering the size of the brigade, sir, you didn't know every -- each and every member of the brigade? Is that correct? You didn't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for many of them, you didn't know what battalion, what company they were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes, a battalion or a company?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question was probably not sufficiently clear. You -- you wouldn't know for all the 3.000 or so men which you said composed the 9th Brigade which particular battalion or which particular company they were members of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor do you know the name -- all the names and identity of those members of the 9th Brigade who were sent to Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor would you know for all of them or perhaps even for the majority of them which company or which part of the brigade they were members of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know, for instance -- or should I ask you it that way: Do you know in what battalion Mr. Turkovic was a member of? Do you know that or not??

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I think it was an engineers unit. I happen to know him, and I think he belonged to the engineers company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Crni, a man by the nickname Crni; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would individuals named Suljo and Regan -- or nicknamed Suljo and Regan also be members of this engineers company, sir?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I don't know those names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies, sir. In October 1993, you were arrested and detained.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that detention, you were interviewed.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person who interviewed you was the name -- was a person named Arnautovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nicknamed Brada.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the first name of that person, sir?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a lawyer present when you were being interviewed by Mr. Arnautovic?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that a fact that Mr. Arnautovic used illegal means during this interview, that he threatened you physically and also threatened your career as a -- as a lawyer? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that when you were released, you heard from other members of the 9th Brigade that similar measures had been used against them during those interviews?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. That will be all for the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, there is. Thank you, Your Honours. Re-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapur, my learned colleague asked you a moment ago about when you were in detention when you were interviewed. When you said you were in detention, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: During the Trebevic operation, I was wounded, which is why I was hospitalised for a week. I was formally listed as detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But where were you actually staying at the time when you were interviewed in December 1993? Were you in a detention facility or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I was not in detention. I was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying it was a form of house arrest or just a -- a way of describing your status, that is, "in detention"?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: No, it was not house arrest. I didn't know what my position was at all at that time. As far as I know, I was not under house arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about the criminality of the 9th Motorised Brigade, and you said that it was not a criminal brigade as such but some individuals in it were. And you said there were very few bad soldiers, and you named some, including Hota and Kenan. You were also asked about whether any serious criminal offences were committed by soldiers within the 9th before September 1993 -- or whether you were aware of any. And you said "no." Now, what I want to clarify is what did you -- what is your understanding of "serious criminal offences"? What do you -- what did you mean when you answered no to that?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: It's common knowledge what serious criminal offences are. I know that certain individuals from the brigade misused their weapons by going, for example, to public markets where civilians were selling goods in order to survive, to earn a living, and that they literally robbed them of their goods and did what they wanted with those goods, sold them or -- I don't know what. So I was not aware of any murders or rapes or serious robberies. I only know that certain individuals engaged in petty criminal activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to clarify what you mean by "petty criminal activities," in your statement which is your evidence here, at paragraph 13 you referred to "soldiers from the assault company introducing themselves as military police and extorting money from citizens in Sarajevo." And you referred to a person called Medeni informing you that --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We object to that. I mean, this is a piece of evidence which is indeed in the witness statement which became the evidence in chief of the Prosecution. He was not cross-examined on that incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, but I believe that, you know, this kind of evidence is just a natural follow-up from the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, the witness was cross-examined in relation to donations in general. There was no queries in relation to any particular incident which is listed in the Prosecution statement. We would submit that this witness could be asked general questions as to the matter of donations but that no specific incident can be touched upon in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, that's just incorrect. My learned friend cross-examined him about a very specific incident in here, relating to someone called --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, that's the only incident which he was cross-examined upon, Your Honour. That's correct. Not this one. Not the one which the Prosecution is trying to lead now in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't know how my learned friend knows because I hadn't actually finished the question. If he'd let me finish the question, I might have got to the point of the clarification of what "petty criminal activities" meant. If I could be allowed to finish it, I'll get to that point fairly quickly, and I would have done so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll see how far you could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll see how far you could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapur, I'm trying to clarify what you mean by "petty criminal activities." In your statement, which is your evidence, you referred to the extortion of money from citizens in Sarajevo by members of the assault company. You referred to a person called Medeni saying that he had been brought -- that money had been taken from him by Mustafa Hota and Kenan. You referred to the theft of an UNPROFOR car by Mustafa Hota --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we really insist with this -- with this objection. I mean, the Prosecution is trying to lead evidence in re-examination which it -- it should have put and it has, as a matter of fact, put in the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I please finish my question without you interrupting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as a rule, Mr. Re, you are allowed to ask some questions about extortions. But the theft of the car by Hota is in the direct examination. So just narrow your scope of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My clarification -- I will certainly do that. For the Trial Chamber's benefit is only to clarify what the witness means by "petty criminal activities." And if the things he referred to in his statement are in fact petty criminal activities. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- As far as I want to take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could ask a general question and let the witness answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I be permitted to give him his statement? It would be much quicker -- and if say, "Look at paragraph 13, point 1, point 2, point 3, and are the things listed there referred --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid not because we have already admitted that evidence, and we're not going to revisit it at redirect examination. The redirect examination should be strictly within the scope of the cross-examination. But anyway, you have the full right to clarify certain issues which were mentioned in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a general proposition, Mr. Kapur, are the things you referred to in your statement which is your evidence in chief and the specific matter upon which Mr. Mettraux cross-examined you, did you consider those to be petty criminal matters? The matters I mentioned earlier: The car, the extortion, the taking civilians to the front line and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, there again we have to object. The car make a new appearance. The Prosecution could ask a very simple question: Sir, what did you understand by "petty criminality"?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I must be entitled to clarify whether what is in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- evidence in chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But you just ask a general question and let the witness answer what is his understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood your question. Please allow me to answer. You said that they committed crimes. In the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina, "crimes" imply serious crimes, such as murders, rapes, robberies, armed robberies, and so on. I just wish to draw a distinction between those kinds of crimes and petty crimes. Petty crimes are also crimes. I'm speaking now as a lawyer. But the sanctions prescribed by the law for such crimes are smaller. If during the war an armed soldier steals a sack of potatoes from a market stall, that is not a serious crime; it's a petty crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My learned friend also cross-examined you about taking civilians to the front line. In the context of your last answer, did you also consider that to be a petty criminal matter?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I would call that a petty crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also answered in response to a question from Mr. Mettraux --

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: May I explain why I say that? When these instances happened of taking civilians to dig trenches by the 9th Motorised Brigade, those people were absolutely protected. They were given a meal. And this was very important during the war when there was no food. And they were also given a box of -- a packet of cigarettes, which cost 20 German marks in Sarajevo at the time. So in that way, they were paid in a way for what they were doing. And not a single civilian was wounded or killed on the line of the 9th Brigade, as far as I know. Had someone been killed, then I would have considered it a serious crime. But if nobody suffered any consequences, then I do not consider it a serious crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also answered in response to a question from Mr. Mettraux about Ramiz Delalic, Celo's tolerance of legal activities. You said: "To agree" -- sorry, that he would not tolerate it. You said: "To a degree, that was correct." I just want to qualify with you: What do you mean by "to a degree that was correct"? What sort of criminal activities or illegal activities would or did Mr. Delalic tolerate?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Well, let's say that he tolerated people being taken to dig trenches, but he did not tolerate someone going and committing a robbery. For example, what I said in my statement, that they robbed Medeni, the persons I named, and Ramiz Delalic when he learned that they had done that and that they had said that he sent them to do it, he personally punished them for that by bringing one of them into detention where I was, and he was there for 20 days in detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In cross-examination about Mr. Nedzad Burovic who had his vehicle taken from him and you said that Mr. Delalic ordered that he go to the trenches, I think for a day, did Mr. Burovic voluntarily go to the trenches to do digging or did he just want --

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- his --

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you're saying that he went there because he wanted his vehicle back or because he wanted to go there?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: He went in order to get his vehicle back, and he was happy to have his vehicle back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also in cross-examination in response to questions about Mr. Delalic's attitude to other soldiers, Mr. Mettraux asked you about JNA officers and you said that he didn't like former -- he didn't like former JNA officers. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I remember in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic was, of course, a former JNA officer --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I please finish the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No, no, you can't. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I please ask the direction that I be entitled to finish the question before my friend objects?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe there's something very important in your question which triggered the objection. Is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We haven't asked any specifics, other than Mr. Imsirovic as a JNA officer. And the question was of a very general nature, and it's not the place in re-examination now to try to have this witness give evidence about the relationship between Mr. Halilovic or the alleged relationship and members of the 9th Brigade, whoever they -- they would be. This -- the place to do so, if that's the Prosecution's intention, was examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with the objections. It is not a right place to have some evidence concerning with the relationship between those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is Your Honour is referring to Mr. Halilovic? I actually hadn't finished my question. And I'd -- really would ask as a matter of professional courtesy that I complete the question before I -- an objection is made. And then I would respond to it, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe you could put your question another way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kapur, you gave evidence that Celo, Ramiz Delalic, did not like JNA officers. Which JNA officers do you know that he didn't like?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I know that he did not like Muslimovic, Jasarevic, and generally speaking he did not respect JNA officers, with the exception of Mr. Sefer Halilovic, whom he respected as a commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also asked about the money that was available to the ABiH. The question was: There was very little money available to the ABiH. That was your answer. My question to you is -- for clarification is: Were you aware in 1993 of the sources of funding of the ABiH, whether internal or external? Or what was the state of your awareness or otherwise of that?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I don't know how the Army of BH was funded, and I said that I knew about Sarajevo but not about the BH army. Sarajevo was closed, and I knew that there was a lack of ammunition, a lack of food, a lack of medicines. But I wasn't aware of the sources of funding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux also cross-examined you about the collection of money from people to "donate" to the 9th Motorised Brigade, and you said that only a minority of people were actually collecting money for the 9th Motorised Brigade. What was your knowledge about whether or not these people were giving all of the money they got from business people to the 9th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I know that a minority of those people got funds in that way. They would bring to the brigade command or to the -- this assault detachment people who had businesses during the war, who had hotels, restaurants, and so on. And they had to give a certain amount of money to the brigade. But I don't know who they gave the money to, nor was I ever present when somebody gave money to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence in cross-examination, in response to Mr. Mettraux's questions, was that these people, as far as you knew, in response to a specific proposition put to you, only collected money from profiteers. In the context of your evidence here, were Medeni, Druskic, and Semso, did you consider them to be profiteers?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, just a clarification so that the question is not put unfairly to the witness. I believe the question to have been that they were regarded as war profiteers by the people from whom the money was collected. And I think the -- the question should be rephrased in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't know how else the witness could perceive the question.

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I understood the question. I will explain. A certain Medeni, who was mentioned, had a restaurant throughout the war. He wasn't engaged as a member of the B and H army, and it was common knowledge that he was earning a lot of money then when the people in question went and extorted the money from him, they probably believed him to be a profiteer, because it was common knowledge in Sarajevo about who was a profiteer and who wasn't. Profiteers were all of those who were involved in business in Sarajevo but were not involved in the combat activities. But they did it on their own. I personally saw that Ramiz Delalic was not aware of that. And when I intervened with Ramiz Delalic, a large quantity of money and valuables were returned to Medeni, while some of it remained at the brigade, and he received receipt and note of thanks for being a donor. There was another person called Semso. He was a butcher. He was also treated as a profiteer in Sarajevo. In that way, they probably considered him to be a profiteer and they also took a certain quantity of money from him as well. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the motel owner, Druskic? Was he in the same category?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Druskic? Yes, he was also well known as a profiteer. He feels involved in large business deals and he was considered to be a profiteer in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My learned colleague Mr. Mettraux also asked you about your obligations as the chief of the military police company and specifically your obligations to investigate crime. You said that -- to the effect, you didn't consider you had an obligation to investigate crime. What -- what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: We had jurisdiction within the 9th Motorised Brigade, but then within the military police you also had the crimes department. There were four or five people working there who had been trained adequately for that and who, according to instructions of Tomo Juric, the chief of security, dealt with violations of discipline by members of the brigade. For example, if a soldier did not report to the line or did not report for guard duty, Tomislav Juric would issue instructions to the military police or to the crimes section, and then we would just carry out his orders. We were not authorised to investigate or to undertake any measures independently; we, the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux also cross-examined you about the blockade of Central -- of some parts of the centre of Sarajevo in July 1993 by members of the 9th and 10th Brigades. In one of your answers, you said: "I did not see how those policemen" - meaning civilian policemen - "were disarmed and brought in." Where were they brought into and who were these civilian police?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I didn't see the civilian police officers whom they disarmed, but I heard it from other soldiers or through the radio communications, because I did have a hand-held radio, a Motorola. I didn't see that personally. I didn't see the blockade of the police station or the disarming of the police officers personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said was that they were disarmed and brought in. What I'm trying to clarify is: Where were they brought into? What do you mean by "brought in"?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I don't know where they were taken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know they were brought in somewhere?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: I'm saying that I heard that from other soldiers or through the radio communications, that they had been disarmed and brought in. They were not at the military police where I was, so I don't know where they were taken. There were two members who were brought from the Laste Special Unit in the meantime. That was a military unit. When I arrived, I ordered that they should be released. No one else had been brought to the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just a little bit confused. Are you referring to the same two people there, or is it two sets of two police?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: Two people, I'm thinking -- I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first one you said were not taken to the military police. Then you said when you arrived, you ordered that two members of the Laste Special Unit be released. Are you referring to two different police who were brought in later?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: No. No. I'm thinking of the same people. But you didn't state it properly a little bit earlier. You asked me where the civilian police officers were brought in. And what I said was I didn't know where they were brought in but that I know these two police officers whom I'm speak about were brought in when I wasn't at the military police and then I ordered them to be released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Released from where?

utterances.speaker: KEMO KAPUR
utterances.text: To be released from detention and to go on about their business. To be freed so that they are no longer in the military police building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That completes my re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any documents to tender through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. Madam Usher will show you out of the room, and we wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that we should have some discussions about the next witness. Yes, who will deal with the next witness? Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. Yes, I will. Oh, I understand that there may be some confusion about whether this next witness, Mr. Emin Zebic is going to be -- his evidence will be led live or via Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The Prosecution intends to lead his evidence live, unless there are objection from my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, after some discussions took place with the Prosecutors, we have decided to agree to -- or to not object. Though I think the -- I think the order of things is that the Prosecutors have to make a formal application, although it was foreshadowed by Mr. -- Mr. Weiner on a previous occasion. We've now had time to think about the position and -- well, without going into discussions, the fact is we don't oppose the application that the Prosecutor is now about to make to have that witness heard live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. You want to have a reply or comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No, that's fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this Bench noted that the Defence does not object to the application of the Prosecutor to vary its witness list to add Zebic on the list of live witnesses. The Trial Chamber has reviewed the statements of this witness and considers that the statements of this witness goes to the acts and the conduct of the accused. In particular, the knowledge of the accused that crimes were committed. And may provide evidence which is very important to this case. Therefore, in full recognition of the rights of the accused to a fair and expeditious trial, the Bench grants the Prosecution's application to vary its 65 ter witness list so that Zebic will be heard as a live witness. In light of this decision, the Bench considers the Prosecution's motion to admit the statement of this witness pursuant to Rule 92 bis to be moot. It is so decided. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Sachdeva:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zebic.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name, your date, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Emin Zebic, 24th of April, 1945.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you some -- some questions about your personal background, and I will lead this evidence from you. You have lived in Jablanica all your life; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1968 to 1969, you were in the JNA at the school of reserve officers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1976 to 1980, you studied as the Faculty of Political Science in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, that is, 1976 to 1981, you were also the chief of police at Jablanica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1981 to 1984, you were president of the executive committee in Jablanica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from 1985 to 1992, you worked for the enterprise called Granit and you were the manager and chief of development during that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 8th of May, 1992 you were the chief of police at the SJB, chief of police in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Presently you are on the verge of retirement; is that right? From that position.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm now going to ask you some questions about the police station in Jablanica. First of all, can you describe -- or tell the Court the area of responsibility of your police station during -- during the war, that is, 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: The Jablanica Public Security Station covered the municipality of Jablanica, meaning that it had police jurisdiction over that territory, the territory of the municipality of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which police station or institution was the Jablanica police responsible to?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: The Jablanica Public Security Station was part of the Minister of Internal Affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The higher instance of territorial organisation than the public security station would be the Centre for Public Security with headquarters in Mostar, and then the Minister for Internal Affairs, which had its headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of a village called Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time of September 1993, which area in terms of policing did Grabovica fall under?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: In terms of policing, since the municipal boarders were not changed, the village of Grabovica belonged to the municipality of Mostar. The public security station was from the territorial aspect in charge of policing in the village of Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you've told us that Jablanica police station was also responsible to the police security service in Mostar, please tell the Court whether you, as chief of police in Jablanica, had a responsibility over Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I said that the police station in Mostar was in charge of Jablanica while the public security centre was my superior. It was also headquartered in Mostar. In 1993, the public security station in Jablanica did not have any jurisdiction in the village of Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a police station in Grabovica, if you know, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: The closest police station was in the village of Dreznica, which is to the south of the village of Grabovica, but this was a reserve police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to ask you some questions about Grabovica. In September 1993, who was living in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: In September 1993, the inhabitants of Grabovica were exclusively of Croat ethnicity. At that time, there were perhaps several hundred Bosniaks in Grabovica also who were refugees from Capljina and Stolac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "inhabitants of Grabovica who were exclusively of Croat ethnicity," are you referring to civilians or military personnel?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking about the population. That's the civilian population. As I said, the original inhabitants were exclusively of Croat ethnicity and then there were also some Bosniaks who were accommodated there, but all the citizens, all the inhabitants were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September 1993, which army controlled Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: In September 1993, the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you know, whereabouts in the village of Grabovica were the Croat inhabitants living?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: The Croat inhabitants were living on the left and the right bank of the Neretva River. On both banks of the river -- both banks of the river were inhabited by ethnic Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a similar question for the Bosniak refugees from Capljina and Stolac: Which side predominantly were they living on?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they, too, were accommodated on both banks, but predominantly on the left bank of the river because there was some prefabricated huts that were empty from -- that were used earlier on construction sites, and that's where they were billeted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want you to cast your mind back to the 9th of September, 1993. In the morning of that day, did anybody come and visit the police station in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Two young women, two Bosniak women came from amongst the expelled Bosniak population, and they came to the Jablanica police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to them?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I personally did not speak to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who spoke to them?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: The duty officer at the reception area of the Jablanica police station did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what these two women said to the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: My deputy, the deputy chief of security of the public security station in Jablanica, after they had already left, told me that they had reported that in Jablanica the night before, mostly on the right bank, some firing, quite loud firing was heard from firearms. And they thought, or that they heard that some inhabitants of Grabovica were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go through that slowly. First of all, can you tell the Court, please, who -- well, the name of your deputy.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: My deputy's name is Ahmed Salihamidzic. I have to say that was his name because he has for some time now been out of the police service. He's no longer serving in the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you know, did these two females speak to your deputy, at that time, when they came into the station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if he spoke to them or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he get this information from these two women?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just intervene there. Pardon me. I don't think this witness says that Salihamidzic is the person who got the information from these women. He says that -- Mr. Zebic says that he got the information from Mr. Salihamidzic, but he hasn't said yet where Mr. Salihamidzic got that information himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe -- yes, I believe there's some misunderstandings between the counsel and the witness. Am I right, Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that the witness said that the females gave information to the duty officer. And then when I asked him how he knew this information, he spoke about his deputy. So I -- my next question was whether the females actually spoke as well to the deputy as well. But I -- but I can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There's no objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how did your deputy, Mr. Salihamidzic, learn of this information?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: All reports arriving in the public security station are recorded in the logbook kept by the duty officer who receives the reports. My deputy read what was recorded in the logbook and informed me about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the duty officer record what these women told him?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, because that's the procedure. All events are to be recorded in the daily logbook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you learned that there was firing from the right-hand side of the bank in Grabovica. This is what these two women told your police station. Were you aware of any soldiers at Grabovica at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I heard that there were some soldiers in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these soldiers from, if you know?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I heard that some units from Sarajevo had arrived in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hear this from?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: As the chief of the public security station, I was also a member of the War Presidency of the municipality. Almost always the commander of the local brigade of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was invited to attend sessions of the War Presidency, so that the Presidency would be informed of any needs of the local brigade and other issues of interest to the civilian authorities. Besides this, cooperation between the public security station and the 44th Mountain Brigade, which was the local unit in the area, was something that went on on an almost daily basis, and it was from these sources that I knew about the facts you have just asked me about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I will ask you about the 44th Mountain Brigade later on, but for now did you know the names of the brigade -- names of the brigades that were in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't know the names and numbers of the units that were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out later?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find out?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: First of all, some hours after the event you have asked me about, the commander of one of those units came to see me with his deputy. After the following events that happened on that day, my deputy told me about the contacts he had had in the area and the information he had obtained and also about the units that were down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the commander of one of those units came to see you with his deputy," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Edib Saric, who commanded a small unit called the Igman Wolves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: They were located in the business premises of the Grabovica hydroelectric power plant on the left bank of the Neretva at the entrance to the village of Grabovica on the north side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can recall, when -- well, what time did they come and see you and your deputy at the police station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: This was around noon or maybe 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, what was the date, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: The 9th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they came to the police station, what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: They told me that they, too, had heard shooting during the night on the right bank of the Neretva and that they thought that there had been civilian victims on that bank of the river, that there had been murders, civilians who had been murdered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you know, what was the basis of their thinking that civilians had been murdered?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I do know that from where they were, they could certainly have heard the shooting, in view of the distance dividing the location where they were billeted and where the other units were billeted on the right bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, upon learning of this information from Grabovica, first from the two women and then from the commander of -- and the deputy of the Igman -- Igman's Wolves, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I discussed with my deputy what we should do, because this was not in our area of responsibility. On the other hand, it was the area of responsibility of the military structures, including our 44th Mountain Brigade with which we had frequent, almost daily contacts. In the end, we agreed that we should try contacting the commander of the military police company of the 44th Brigade to see what they thought about it and to have the information checked. The commander of the military police company - and I assume he had the approval of his brigade commander - came to see us and he was willing to go to the scene of these events with my deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just to be clear, who was the commander of the 44th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: At that time, the commander of the 44th was Enes Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you know, which corps did the 44th Mountain Brigade fall within?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the military police -- military police company of the 44th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: The commander of the military police company was Sead Kurt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to ask you what happened after you contacted the -- Mr. Kurt. But since you've mentioned the 44th Mountain Brigade, let's move on to that topic. Where were they located, firstly?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: The command was in Jablanica, in the town of Jablanica. Perhaps 100 metres away from the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the 44th Mountain Brigade the only military presence in Jablanica at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I can't be certain, but at the time I know there was a forward command post there of the Supreme Command Staff of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you know, where was the forward command post situated?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: The forward command post was in the building of Elektroprivreda, or rather, the administration building of the Jablanica hydroelectric power plant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was at that post at the time? And when I say "at that time," I don't mean specifically on the 9th September but generally in and around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I think my learned friend has to be specific about the time that he's referring to there. He doesn't have to limit it to the 9th, but he has to set proper parameters, bearing in behind what's said about the presence of the accused at various meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, how about at beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, from the beginning of September, who was at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know that, nor can I know something like that. I did not know who the members of the forward command post were. They were a military formation and had nothing to do with the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know there was a forward command post in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Jablanica is a very small place, three or four thousand inhabitants concentrated in several square kilometres along the main road. It wasn't difficult to know that. And I have also just mentioned that the public security station cooperated very well with the 44th Mountain Brigade and also that I was a member of the War Presidency of Jablanica municipality, so that I knew that, as did many of the inhabitants of Jablanica municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that -- although you couldn't be certain, but you said that there was a forward command post from the Supreme Command Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you know why there was a forward command post in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak into the microphone, please. The interpreters did not hear the reply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps this is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, could we have a break. And we'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Sachdeva, please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, just before we -- we had a break, I asked you how you knew there was a forward command post in Jablanica, and you told the Court that the public security station cooperated very well with the 44th Mountain Brigade and also that "I was a member of the War Presidency of Jablanica -- of the Jablanica municipality, so I knew that, as did many of the inhabitants of Jablanica municipality." On that day, the 9th of September, did you go to the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the head of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Dr. Safet Cibo was the president of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went there, did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I spoke to Dr. Cibo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I told him about what I had heard up to that point as to what had happened in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: As I told him about this after my deputy had returned from a patrol to Grabovica, I conveyed to him what my deputy had told me, that is, that he had confirmed that something had happened there and that the remaining inhabitants on the right bank asked that they be taken out of Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Zebic, I will actually ask you more detail about the visit of your deputy to the village soon, and I will try and have the Court know about that. But right now I'm interested in your conversation with Mr. Cibo when you went to the War Presidency. When you told him about what had happened or what you had learnt that day in Grabovica, what did he say to you, if anything, or what did he do?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: He right away called by telephone somebody, as far as I could understand, at the forward command post and asked about this. He asked for fuller information about what had happened there, down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when he made that phone call?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've got a matter of law to raise here. It's no difficulty with what the witness is saying. I'm just not sure what -- my friend has led this evidence, and I just don't see any reference to it in the proofing notes at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that must be something in the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want to clarify what it is, if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- this information is indeed in his statement he gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 25th of November, 2000, to Mr. Mikhailov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. To my understanding, that if there's anything new to the statement, that should be added in the proofing notes. Otherwise, we'll rely on the previous statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand what my friend is pointing to, and I put a sinister cast on something which I think on reflection is not sinister at all, so I withdraw the objection, and frankly my friend can proceed with that questioning. He's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. You may proceed, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you have to repeat your question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when Mr. Cibo made that phone call to the IKM?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who he spoke to, Mr. Cibo?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I don't know who he spoke to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to the visit of your deputy to Grabovica. Who did he go there with?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: He went there with the commander of the military police company of the 44th Mountain Brigade, Mr. Sead Kurt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did they go there for? Roughly.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: About two or three hours. Thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they returned -- well, did they return to the police station after that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: My deputy returned to the public security station and informed me about what he had done there -- or rather, what he had seen and heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he put that information in writing at any time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, he wrote an official note in connection with this visit and some later activities that he himself conducted, operative activities to gather information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this official note went to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I received this official note.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I will show you that note hereafter. But I now want to stay with the 9th September, on that day, and ask you about a meeting you had after you went to the -- the Presidency -- the War Presidency that day. After that, did anybody else visit the police station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: At around 2000 hours, my minister, Mr. Bakir Alispahic, arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did he come to your police station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: A few days previously, he had taken a unit of the Ministry of the Interior to Mostar to assist the public security services centre there. In view of the fact that to reach Mostar from Jablanica you had to go on foot over mountain crags, he stayed there for a few days and on that day, the 9th of September, he came back across Mount Prenj to Jablanica, and then he dropped into the public security station. He was on his way to Sarajevo. He was passing through, in other words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know beforehand that he was going to visit your police station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I assumed he might drop in on the way back because it was customary, but I didn't know he would be there at that time on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When he came to the police station, did you have a conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had a conversation with him in my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I informed him about everything I knew up to that point about what had been happening in the village of Grabovica and, of course, about other issues having to do with the public security station. He was my superior, and it was my duty to inform him of all these issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you informed him about what had been happening in the village of Grabovica, what was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: He asked that if possible I get a connection for him with somebody from the forward command post of the army, and I did this through my communications centre in the public security station, and this was by telephone, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your communications centre have the telephone number of the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: We were linked up. It was a small area. We had telephone communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he asked you to get a connection with somebody at the forward command post, did he ask for anybody in particular?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He asked to speak to Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who Sefer Halilovic was?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Of course I knew, because Mr. Halilovic was one of the well-known military authorities at the time, and as far as I personally was concerned, he was the best-known military authority in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you -- well, I withdraw that. When you asked your duty officer -- your communications officer to put the call in to the forward command post, did you know that Sefer Halilovic was there at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Of course I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you anticipate that he would be there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, some remote questions can be asked. That one is too remote, whether he would anticipate that he was going to be there or not, in my submission, can't assist and shouldn't be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I withdraw that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to the -- to the conversation. So you asked your communications officer to -- after Mr. Alispahic asked to speak to Mr. Halilovic, you asked your communications officer to connect to the forward command post. Was the connection made?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, the communication was made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the communication made with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, once again, this question is put in a very general way. It's quite obvious that the questions can be asked as to what he heard, said, and -- and the witness is entitled to give evidence about what he heard and what he saw, and that's what he should be asked. When it's put in that way, this Tribunal is not going to know what the basis of the witness's answer is, whether it's on something that he assumes or whether it's on something that he saw. Now, I've got no objection at all to the witness saying what he heard and what he saw, and that seems to be what the question ought to be, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I see no problem with this question, because the witness answered that the communication was made. Then the Prosecution asked who was the communication made with. That's quite, you know, natural. Maybe there will be some follow-up questions about the contents of this communication later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's the basis of the witness's knowledge, but I hear what Your Honour says about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'll extract the basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the connection was made, were you present at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the same room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, who else was in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bakir Alispahic, the minister of the interior, and me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who first spoke to the person on the other end of the line?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: The minister spoke directly to the person at the other end of the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he address that person?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I think he said, "Sefer" when addressing that person, and then continued the conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far were you from Mr. Alispahic when he said "Sefer"?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: About 3 metres away, across the table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Alispahic say to Sefer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness hasn't given evidence that he was talking to Sefer. He's just given evidence that the first thing was said by -- by Mr. Alispahic was "Sefer," that he addressed the person as "Sefer" when he started. So that in my submission the witness can be asked what Mr. Alispahic said and take it from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe you could lead this witness step by step.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Alispahic say?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I can't recall all the words he said, but I do remember that he conveyed in essence what I had told him about the events in Grabovica. And he gave his opinion that this case should be investigated and that other necessary measures should be taken. He said he was willing to involve the police to assist the military security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When that conversation proceeded, what was your understanding as to who Mr. Alispahic was talking to?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I was convinced he was speaking to Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the conversation last?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Maybe two or three minutes. Not longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me just confer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, can I just take you back briefly. You told us that you were convinced that he was speaking to Mr. Sefer Halilovic. Why were you convinced?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Because I heard -- I heard him saying into the receiver "Sefer."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When the conversation ended, what did Mr. Alispahic say?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: He said that he had spoken to Mr. Halilovic, that they had agreed -- or rather, that he had received a promise that the case would be investigated. He gave me oral orders that if any assistance was required from the Jablanica Public Security Station and the police service, that we should provide such assistance to the military security services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any such request for assistance forthcoming?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: No, we never received any such request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the next day, that is, the 10th of September, did anybody not from the station come and visit you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon, the commander of the Zulfikar unit arrived and the commander of the Igmanski Vukovi unit, Mr. Alispago and Mr. Edib Saric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you say they came to see you in the afternoon. Did anybody come and see you in the morning?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: At this moment, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zebic, you told us earlier that your deputy, Mr. Salihamidzic, prepared a report. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that you saw that report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a report is produced by somebody in your station, who is ultimately responsible for releasing that report?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I was, as the chief of the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the witness be shown MFI222, that is, 222. It's actually D149.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can we have the English page 3 shown on the screen, please, which should correspond to the B/C/S page 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, can you read the first line of what you see on your screen, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I can see the first page of the official note here -- or rather, yes, my deputy's official note.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to go to the last page, please. Do you see the paragraph where it says: "At around 8.30 on the 10th of September, 1993 ..."? Do you see that paragraph there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Excuse me, but you asked me whether anybody visited me in the morning, but this was actually in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Who visited you -- who visited you in the evening?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I had two visits: One at approximately 1830 hours, the one by Mr. Zulfikar Alispago and Edib Saric. The other one was at 2030 hours by Mr. Sejo Brankovic and Namik Dzankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Namik Dzankovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: According to the way Mr. Brankovic introduced him, Mr. Dzankovic was one of the members of the security service of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know his rank. I didn't know it at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he had come from?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: He had come, as I said, from the military security service of the B and H army, the Supreme Command Staff, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you'd go back to the -- to the document -- the report prepared by your deputy, and at the paragraph where I asked you to look at, do you see Mr. Dzankovic's name mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you see where it says: "Together with the IKM, forward command post, security officer Namik Dzankovic."

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any reason for you to doubt that description of Mr. Dzankovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Perhaps if the witness could be just asked a direct question rather than having his hand forced in a leading we. He can be asked what his understanding is of Mr. Dzankovic's role. This is a form of leading. Simply put a document in his hand and say, "Do you agree with that," takes away any weight to the answer, generally speaking. But I would just make the formal objection that he shouldn't lead on a matter like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your understanding, if any, about Mr. Dzankovic's role?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: When he came, together with Mr. Brankovic, who was a police officer whom we knew from before, and he introduced him as an officer of the army security, it was all the same to me what his rank was, whether he was from the IKM or from the Supreme Command Staff. So I can agree with what it says -- what it says here. I have no reason not to believe them if that's how they introduced themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Dzankovic say to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, may I just interrupt --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dzankovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zebic. I just have an objection to make about the question. Your Honours, I'm just wanting to ask whether the Prosecutor is wanting to put this document to the witness and ask him whether he agrees with every word in it one by one, or whether he's going to ask the witness any questions about the witness's own memory of the situation. Because leaving the document in front of the witness has the effect that the witness, quite understandably, is going to look at the document. That's what I would do too, frankly. Now, it depends what my friend's course is going to be. But he should clarify that before I go any further with the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's correct. No, actually it was an oversight. The document can be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The B/C/S version is gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Dzankovic say to you when he came to the station?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: He said that he had come as a member of the army security service to see or to hear which information we had relating to the events in Grabovica. Since my deputy was also present during this conversation, we gave him everything that we knew up to that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On receiving this information from yourself and your deputy, what did Mr. Dzankovic do?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brankovic and he also brought information for us relating to Grabovica. They said that strange things were happening again in Grabovica. And we made a call from there to Mr. Zulfikar Alispago, Zuka. During the telephone conversation, he suggested that Mr. Dzankovic and Brankovic come to visit his base. So from my office, they left to go to Mr. Zulfikar Alispago's base. I know that Mr. Dzankovic went to Mr. Zulfikar Alispago's following that conversation from my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Dzankovic ask you for any assistance?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Of course. The conversation was quite proper. We expressed our readiness to help, and he also sought our help to secure further information required for him to be able to continue his work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the extent of -- of the help he sought from you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Mostly providing information that we had received, and together with my associates, giving him the opportunity possibly to visit the area in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that Mr. Alispahic had -- when he came to visit you had requested of you if you asked to -- to provide assistance to find out what had happened in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell the Court what the station had, in terms of facilities, to assist in any investigation.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: The Jablanica Public Security Station at the time functioned fully. It had a modest amount of equipment, but it had as much as it needed. We had police officers who were trained for on-site investigations and for that time, wartime - that's what I am talking about - we had the required technical equipment, such as cameras, film, and so on, because at that time it was very important to have that. Also, certain testing kits to look at the marks left on the scene of the crime. The Jablanica Public Security Station did have all the essential equipment to conduct an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the use of this equipment that you've described and this type of assistance that you've described, was that ever asked of you from the military?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: No. We never received a request for something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may the witness be shown MFI235. It's D29.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zebic, do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, the beginning of it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the date on that document?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 29th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at that time, did you see this document?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw this document was during the investigations that have taken place recently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Investigations by whom? Just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mikhailov in Sarajevo, when he conducted the interview with me. He showed me the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at the last paragraph of this document, right at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the English page will have to be turned over to get to that in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm grateful to my friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have that there, Mr. Zebic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read that out, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: "The investigation and other expert activities regarding the exhumation will be carried out by the crimes service of the MUP and the military police of Jablanica in cooperation with other experts."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, is this -- is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
utterances.text: I don't think that this stands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN ZEBIC
